data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The dilemma dissolves if we view corroboration not as a measure of truth or probability, but as a report of the current state of critical discussion, making preference a procedural necessity rather than an epistemic inference.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If scientists clearly act on the belief that corroborated theories are more likely to be true, not just procedurally convenient.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the 'game' of science aims at truth, rendering purely procedural rules insufficient for goal attainment.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the severity of a test cannot be assessed without inductive background knowledge.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"Corroboration is purely historical: it reports 'Theory T has been tested and not yet refuted.' It makes no claim about T's future. The preference for T is not an epistemic judgment that T is better, but a procedural rule of the game of science: 'Do not discard a theory that has not been falsified in favor of one that has, or in favor of nothing.' This avoids induction because it makes no prediction; it simply dictates the current move in the dialectic.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
